claims.text: Atomic-level compositional complexity enhances lattice distortion in high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Repeated multilayer interfaces act as strong barriers to dislocation glide or transmission.
Lattice distortion and interface barriers act synergistically to suppress strain accumulation during prolonged loading.
A monolithic HEA coating lacks the additional engineered interfaces present in a multilayer coating.
The absence of engineered multilayer interfaces produces a faster plastic response under load in the monolithic coating.
At identical bulk composition and loading conditions, multilayer coatings will accumulate less creep strain than monolithic HEA coatings.
Multilayer coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to monolithic HEA coatings.
Microscopy should reveal dislocation networks arrested or deflected at multilayer interfaces.
The proposed comparison varies multilayer architecture while holding bulk HEA composition and loading conditions constant.
The hypothesis is limited to stress and temperature regimes that do not cause phase transformations or delamination.
Increasing individual layer thickness reduces interface density.
The proposed mechanism may cease to provide substantial resistance when the layers are too thick.
The proposed mechanism may not govern deformation at extremely high temperatures where diffusion-controlled processes dominate.
The relative contributions of lattice distortion and interface blocking are not quantitatively established.
The interplay between lattice distortion and interface blocking may vary with stress and temperature.
Microstructural evolution during prolonged creep remains insufficiently characterized.
